permitted_combinations_note: Migration (08) is paired with Impact of Empire + Urban Environments: Spitalfields. Power (09) is paired with English Reformation + Castles: Kenilworth. War (10) is paired with Personal Rule to Restoration + Castles: Kenilworth. These pairings are spec-mandated; the browse UI should signal them.

common_misconceptions_subject_wide.misconception: Students rehearse the schools of thought (Orthodox, Revisionist, Post-revisionist for the Cold War; Guilty Men/Popular Majority/Revisionist for Appeasement) but do not anchor each schools view to specific evidence inside the given interpretation extract. Top-band answers quote a phrase from the extract and link it directly to a named historian or school.
common_misconceptions_subject_wide.source: OCR Examiners report J410/02 Summer 2023, ocr.org.uk Images 704672

common_misconceptions_subject_wide.topic: Section A Q3 vs Q4 confusion
common_misconceptions_subject_wide.misconception: Q3 asks what other historians/views would think of the given interpretation (fair or not). Q4 asks the student to evaluate the named interpretation using their own knowledge. Students frequently swap the approaches and waste exam minutes giving the wrong type of analysis.
common_misconceptions_subject_wide.source: OCR Examiners report J410/02 Summer 2023, ocr.org.uk Images 704672

common_misconceptions_subject_wide.topic: Time-frame discipline in period-study outline questions
common_misconceptions_subject_wide.misconception: When asked about US worldwide actions in the 1960s, students offer Marshall Aid or the Truman Doctrine (1940s). Material outside the date range earns no credit even if accurate.
common_misconceptions_subject_wide.source: OCR Examiners report J410/02 Summer 2023, Q1 commentary, ocr.org.uk Images 704672

common_misconceptions_subject_wide.misconception: Students treat the source as information (the source tells us). The 7b utility question rewards inferences supported by the source's content, not provenance lectures and not a parallel essay of contextual knowledge.
common_misconceptions_subject_wide.source: OCR Examiners report J410/02 Summer 2023, Q7b commentary, ocr.org.uk Images 704672

common_misconceptions_subject_wide.topic: Impact vs process in depth-study explain questions
common_misconceptions_subject_wide.misconception: Students describe how a policy was carried out (the process) rather than what changed because of it (the impact). Examiners want a three-stage explanation: identification, specific detail, and change from before.
common_misconceptions_subject_wide.source: OCR Examiners report J410/02 Summer 2023, Q6 'Assessment for learning' box, ocr.org.uk Images 704672

common_misconceptions_subject_wide.misconception: Students offer accurate examples from outside the date range of the question (e.g. answering a Tudor Parliament question with material on Charles I). Examiners explicitly cap such answers at Level 1 even when the history is correct.
common_misconceptions_subject_wide.source: OCR Examiners report J410/09 Summer 2022, Q1 'Advice to centres', ocr.org.uk Images 688215

common_misconceptions_subject_wide.misconception: Students describe a development without analysing it for significance. The mark scheme rewards a deliberate judgement about scale, reach or turning-point effect. Restating the description in different words does not satisfy the AO2 demand.
common_misconceptions_subject_wide.source: OCR Examiners report J410/09 Summer 2022, Q3 commentary, ocr.org.uk Images 688215

common_misconceptions_subject_wide.misconception: Students cover one of the two named periods well and barely touch the other, or argue only one side of the statement. The top band needs balanced coverage across both periods and both sides of the prompt.
common_misconceptions_subject_wide.source: OCR Examiners report J410/09 Summer 2022, paper overview, ocr.org.uk Images 688215

common_misconceptions_subject_wide.topic: Confusing rulers and rebellions across centuries
common_misconceptions_subject_wide.misconception: John gets confused with Charles I (ship money attached to John, Magna Carta attached to Parliament). Edward I gets confused with Edward III. Naming the wrong monarch loses both AO1 and AO2 marks even when the wider point is sound.
common_misconceptions_subject_wide.source: OCR Examiners report J410/09 Summer 2022, Q2 misconception box, ocr.org.uk Images 688215

common_misconceptions_subject_wide.misconception: On Kenilworth or Spitalfields source comparisons students treat the two sources in isolation (paragraph on Source A, paragraph on Source B) rather than weaving them together against an investigation question. The top band rewards integrated comparison.
common_misconceptions_subject_wide.source: OCR J410 specification Section 3a assessment overview, ocr.org.uk gcsehistorymodernworld

examiner_signals_subject_wide.signal: Component 1 Section A Q3 is worth 15 marks and Q4 is worth 25 marks (including 5 SPaG). Combined they are 40 of the 65 Section A marks. Interpretation technique is the highest-leverage skill in the period study.
examiner_signals_subject_wide.source: OCR J410 specification Section 3a question structure, ocr.org.uk gcsehistorymodernworld

examiner_signals_subject_wide.signal: Component 1 Section B (non-British depth study) can be set with either Q7a + Q7b (two 5-mark source questions) or a single Q7 worth 10 marks. Either way two sources are always provided. Centres must drill both shapes.
examiner_signals_subject_wide.source: OCR J410 specification Section 3a paragraph on Q7 variants, ocr.org.uk gcsehistorymodernworld

examiner_signals_subject_wide.signal: Component 2 (thematic) Q4 is a 24-mark essay assessing change and continuity. It can require evidence from two of the three named eras or all three. Students who plan only a two-era answer can be caught short.
examiner_signals_subject_wide.source: OCR J410 specification Section 3a Component 2, ocr.org.uk gcsehistorymodernworld

examiner_signals_subject_wide.signal: Component 3 Section A British depth has only two questions: a 10-mark explain and a 25-mark essay using sources. The 25-mark essay is the single largest question on the qualification by mark value.
examiner_signals_subject_wide.source: OCR J410 specification Section 3a Component 3, ocr.org.uk gcsehistorymodernworld

examiner_signals_subject_wide.signal: Component 3 Section B (historic environment) is a fixed pairing with the British depth study: Spitalfields with Migration (J410/08+11), Kenilworth with Reformation (J410/09+12), Kenilworth with Personal Rule (J410/10+13). Site-specific case-study knowledge is non-negotiable.
examiner_signals_subject_wide.source: OCR J410 specification Section 2c study of the historic environment, ocr.org.uk gcsehistorymodernworld

examiner_signals_subject_wide.signal: SPaG is 5 marks on Component 1 Q4 only. Period-specific terminology and accurate writing matter most on the interpretation essay. No SPaG on Component 2 or Component 3.
examiner_signals_subject_wide.source: OCR J410 specification Section 3a question tables, ocr.org.uk gcsehistorymodernworld

examiner_signals_subject_wide.signal: AO weighting overall: AO1 = 35%, AO2 = 35%, AO3 = 15%, AO4 = 15%. Knowledge and second-order analysis are 70% of the qualification; sources and interpretations are 30%. Content-thin students cannot rescue marks via source skills alone.
examiner_signals_subject_wide.source: OCR J410 specification Section 3b assessment objectives, ocr.org.uk gcsehistorymodernworld

pedagogical_notes.note: EEF 'Improving Literacy in Secondary Schools' (Recommendation 1, disciplinary literacy): teach the discipline-specific way historians read a source rather than leaving these as implicit habits. Sentence stems such as 'This interpretation aligns with the X school because...' scaffold the J410 interpretation skill.
pedagogical_notes.source: Education Endowment Foundation, Improving Literacy in Secondary Schools guidance report, educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk

pedagogical_notes.note: EEF Metacognition and Self-Regulated Learning evidence: model an expert thinking aloud through an interpretation question - how you decide what view it expresses, why an author might hold it, how you weigh it against another. Particularly important for Q3 vs Q4 distinction on J410/02-07.
pedagogical_notes.source: Education Endowment Foundation, Metacognition and Self-Regulated Learning guidance report, educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk

pedagogical_notes.note: Cambridge Assessment research on history examinations identifies comparative judgement (weighing causes, consequences, factors against each other) as the consistently hardest skill at GCSE. This is exactly what J410 Component 1 Q4 (25 marks) and Component 3 Section A Q2 (25 marks) reward.
pedagogical_notes.source: Cambridge Assessment Network and Research, history examinations archive, cambridgeassessment.org.uk

pedagogical_notes.note: OCR centres are advised to teach the British depth study inside the thematic study rather than as a separate block: begin the thematic study, pause when the depth study's window opens, teach the depth study, then resume the thematic study. This keeps the historic environment site embedded in the wider narrative.
pedagogical_notes.source: OCR J410 specification Section 2c Introduction to British depth studies, ocr.org.uk gcsehistorymodernworld

pedagogical_notes.note: DfE Political Impartiality in Schools (Feb 2022): when teaching contested historical episodes (apartheid South Africa, the Holocaust, the partition of Vietnam, the British Empire, civil rights in the USA) teachers must offer balanced views of opposing political positions and present multiple perspectives. Apply throughout this qualification.
pedagogical_notes.source: GOV.UK Political impartiality in schools guidance, Feb 2022

pedagogical_notes.note: BBC editorial guidelines on contested history: prefer the language of testimony and evidence over assertion; quote contemporaries rather than asserting motives; avoid loaded framings (e.g. 'aggression', 'liberation') where the historical community is divided.
pedagogical_notes.source: BBC Editorial Guidelines, section 4 (Impartiality), bbc.co.uk editorialguidelines

article_units.name: International Relations 1918-1975
article_units.subtitle: From Versailles to Vietnam — the unfolding narrative of the twentieth-century international order.
article_units.spec_section_focus: Mandatory period study, Component 1 Section A. All centres take this regardless of depth-study choice. 65 marks, ~1 hour exam time.

lessons.title: The Versailles Peace Settlement 1919
lessons.description: Wilson's Fourteen Points, Big Three compromises and the Treaty of Versailles' verdict on Germany.
spec_references: Conflict and co-operation 1918-1939 — The Versailles Peace Settlement
key_figures: Georges Clemenceau, French PM at Paris
David Lloyd George, British PM at Paris
Vittorio Orlando, Italian PM at Paris
lessons.impartiality_notes: Present both 'Carthaginian peace' (Keynes) and 'too lenient' (Foch, Mantoux) readings. Avoid asserting Versailles caused WWII as inevitability — frame as one factor among several.

lessons.title: The League of Nations in the 1920s
lessons.description: How a wounded league handled Vilna, Corfu and the Geneva Protocol — successes and structural weaknesses.
spec_references: Conflict and co-operation 1918-1939 — the League of Nations in the 1920s
key_figures: Benito Mussolini, Italian PM during Corfu
lessons.impartiality_notes: Acknowledge League humanitarian successes (Nansen passports, slavery commission) alongside political failures. US absence is a structural fact, not a moral verdict on America.

lessons.title: International agreements in the 1920s
lessons.description: Dawes, Locarno, Kellogg-Briand and Young — how the 1920s tried to lock in peace by treaty.
spec_references: Conflict and co-operation 1918-1939 — international agreements in the 1920s (Dawes Plan 1924, Locarno 1925, Kellogg-Briand 1928, Young Plan 1929); attempts at disarmament
key_figures: Frank B. Kellogg, US Secretary of State
lessons.impartiality_notes: Present 'Locarno spring' optimism alongside historians (e.g. Steiner) who see the agreements as fragile from the start.

lessons.title: The Great Depression and the retreat to nationalism
lessons.description: How the Wall Street Crash reshaped European politics and unravelled 1920s internationalism.
spec_references: Conflict and co-operation 1918-1939 — the impact of the worldwide economic depression
lessons.impartiality_notes: Frame the rise of authoritarianism as a multi-causal European phenomenon; avoid suggesting it was inevitable consequence of capitalism failing.

lessons.title: Tension in Europe in the 1930s
lessons.description: Manchuria, Abyssinia, Rhineland, Sudetenland — the League's failures and the road to war.
spec_references: Conflict and co-operation 1918-1939 — Tension in Europe in the 1930s, including the failure of the League of Nations, the policy of Appeasement and outbreak of war in 1939
key_events_dates: 3 Sept 1939 — Britain and France declare war
lessons.impartiality_notes: Examiner reports flag this as a common confusion: students mix 1920s and 1930s crises. Time-frame discipline matters. On appeasement, present both Guilty Men and revisionist (R.A.C. Parker) readings.

lessons.title: Yalta, Potsdam and the changing order 1945-1948
lessons.description: How Allied victory and Soviet occupation of Eastern Europe set the terms of the Cold War.
spec_references: The Cold War in Europe 1945-1961 — Actions of the USSR in Eastern Europe 1945-1948 and response of USA and its allies, including conferences at Yalta and Potsdam
key_events_dates: 1945-48 — Soviet salami tactics across Poland, Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria, Czechoslovakia
key_figures: Franklin D. Roosevelt (Yalta only — died 12 Apr 1945)
Clement Attlee (took over at Potsdam after UK election)
lessons.impartiality_notes: Present orthodox (Soviet expansionism) and revisionist (US power projection / atomic diplomacy) readings as live historical positions, not as the textbook version vs heresy.

lessons.title: Truman Doctrine, Marshall Plan and divided Germany
lessons.description: How US dollars and divided Berlin made the Cold War a concrete European reality.
spec_references: The Cold War in Europe 1945-1961 — The division of Germany; the Truman Doctrine and the Marshall Plan; the Berlin Blockade and Airlift
key_figures: George C. Marshall, US Secretary of State
Lucius D. Clay, US military governor in Germany
lessons.impartiality_notes: Frame Marshall Plan with both 'generous reconstruction' and 'dollar imperialism' (Soviet) viewpoints. Note Czechoslovakia and Poland initially wanted aid but were vetoed by Stalin.

lessons.title: NATO, Warsaw Pact and the Berlin Wall
lessons.description: Hardening of the two blocs and the wall that put barbed wire through a European capital.
spec_references: The Cold War in Europe 1945-1961 — Development of NATO and the Warsaw Pact; the building of the Berlin Wall 1961 and its effects on international relations
key_events_dates: 26 Jun 1963 — Kennedy's 'Ich bin ein Berliner' speech
lessons.impartiality_notes: Present 1956 Hungary as a Soviet repression that constrained the Cold War rules of the game; present Berlin Wall as both 'anti-fascist defence wall' (GDR framing) and tool to halt mass exodus (Western framing).

lessons.title: The Cuban Missile Crisis 1962
lessons.description: Thirteen days that brought the world closest to nuclear war — quarantine, secret diplomacy, climbdown.
spec_references: Cold War confrontations and conflict 1954-1975 — The Cuban Missile Crisis 1962
key_events_dates: Jan 1959 — Castro takes power in Cuba
22 Oct 1962 — Kennedy's TV address, naval quarantine
27 Oct 1962 — Black Saturday, U-2 shot down
1963 — Moscow-Washington hotline; Partial Test Ban Treaty
key_figures: Anatoly Dobrynin, Soviet ambassador to USA
lessons.impartiality_notes: The secret Jupiter missile deal (US removal of missiles from Turkey) was only declassified later — treat its absence from the 1962 public record as a teaching point about historical sources, not as US deception.

lessons.title: US involvement in Vietnam 1954-1965
lessons.description: From Eisenhower's advisers to LBJ's combat troops — how containment dragged America into a land war in Asia.
spec_references: Cold War confrontations and conflict 1954-1975 — Origins of US involvement in Vietnam 1954-65
key_events_dates: May 1954 — Dien Bien Phu, French defeat
Jul 1954 — Geneva Accords, Vietnam divided at 17th parallel
1955 — Diem becomes President of South Vietnam
Nov 1963 — Kennedy assassinated, LBJ takes office
Mar 1965 — Operation Rolling Thunder begins, first combat troops at Da Nang
key_figures: Ho Chi Minh, North Vietnamese leader
Ngo Dinh Diem, South Vietnamese President
lessons.impartiality_notes: Present US involvement through containment logic (domino theory) and contemporary anti-war analysis (e.g. Fulbright hearings 1966) as competing readings; do not editorialise on motive.

lessons.title: The Vietnam War 1965-1973
lessons.description: Search and destroy, Tet, My Lai, Vietnamisation — US tactics, Vietcong tactics and their consequences.
spec_references: Cold War confrontations and conflict 1954-1975 — The Vietnam War: US tactics and their consequences; Vietcong tactics and their consequences; US withdrawal from Vietnam including opposition in the USA to the war
key_events_dates: 1965-68 — General Westmoreland's search and destroy strategy
Mar 1968 — LBJ announces he will not seek re-election
Mar 1973 — Last US combat troops leave
key_figures: Vo Nguyen Giap, North Vietnamese general
lessons.impartiality_notes: Sensitive ground. Present Vietcong tactics (tunnels, guerrilla warfare, terror against village headmen) and US tactics (Agent Orange, napalm, free-fire zones) factually. Avoid characterising either side as 'aggressor' — that is the historiographic question, not the textbook starting point.

lessons.title: End of the war and its international legacy
lessons.description: Fall of Saigon, détente and shifting interpretations of the Cold War after 1975.
spec_references: Cold War confrontations and conflict 1954-1975 — The end of the war and its impact on international relations
Historical controversy — Changing interpretations of Appeasement; Changing interpretations of the responsibility for the Cold War
key_events_dates: 1979 — Soviet invasion of Afghanistan ends détente
Post-1990 — opening of Soviet archives reshapes Cold War historiography
key_figures: Gerald Ford, US President at fall of Saigon
lessons.impartiality_notes: This lesson is partly about historiography itself. Present orthodox / revisionist / post-revisionist Cold War schools as legitimate intellectual positions. On appeasement, present 'Guilty Men' (Foot/Owen), Popular Majority (Taylor) and revisionist (Parker) schools the same way. Examiner reports specifically reward students who can name these schools.

article_units.name: China 1950-1981: The People and the State
article_units.subtitle: Mao's revolution, the Cultural Revolution and Deng's reforms — a society remade three times in thirty years.
article_units.spec_section_focus: Non-British depth study, Component 1 Section B. 40 marks, ~45 minutes exam time. Paired with International Relations 1918-1975.

lessons.title: Establishing communist rule and early purges
lessons.description: How the new PRC consolidated power through land reform, mass campaigns and political terror.
spec_references: Establishing Communism in China 1950-1965 — Early purges against opposition in the 1950s in the cities, countryside and regions
key_events_dates: 1950-52 — Agrarian Reform Law and land redistribution
lessons.impartiality_notes: Use Communist Party language ('campaigns') alongside scholarly estimates of executions (Frank Dikötter, Roderick MacFarquhar). Present land reform's reception by peasants as mixed, not uniformly enthusiastic.

lessons.title: Hundred Flowers and Anti-Rightist Campaigns
lessons.description: Mao invites criticism, then crushes it — the political reversal that defined the second half of the 1950s.
spec_references: Establishing Communism in China — intentions and impact of the Hundred Flowers campaign
key_figures: Deng Xiaoping, ran the Anti-Rightist Campaign as General Secretary
Chu Anping, editor branded a rightist
lessons.impartiality_notes: Historians disagree on whether Mao planned a trap from the outset or genuinely sought criticism then changed course. Present both readings (MacFarquhar vs others).

lessons.title: Social policies, women and education under Mao
lessons.description: Marriage Law, the iron rice bowl and rewriting school curricula — how the state reshaped the family.
spec_references: Establishing Communism in China — Communist social policies under Mao and how these differed from Chinese traditionalism; policies towards women, young people and education
key_events_dates: May 1950 — Marriage Law of the PRC
1952 — Higher education reorganised on Soviet model
key_figures: Soong Ching-ling, women's leader and Vice-President
Deng Yingchao, women's activist (Zhou Enlai's wife)
lessons.impartiality_notes: Present 1950 Marriage Law as a genuine legal change for many women and as policy that remained patchily enforced in rural areas. Avoid 'the Party liberated women' framing without nuance.

lessons.title: The Great Leap Forward and the famine
lessons.description: Backyard furnaces, communes and a famine that killed tens of millions — Mao's deadliest economic experiment.
spec_references: Establishing Communism in China — agricultural policies, including early land reform, collectivisation and its impact; industrial policy, including the First Five Year Plan; the Great Leap Forward, its effect across Chinese society and reasons for failure; Dazhai Commune as a case study
key_events_dates: Jul 1959 — Lushan Conference, Peng Dehuai purged
key_figures: Peng Dehuai, defence minister purged for criticising the Leap
Liu Shaoqi, eventually distanced from policy
lessons.impartiality_notes: Cite Dikötter, Yang Jisheng and Becker for famine death-toll range; present the Party's contemporary line ('three years of natural disaster') as one historical position critiqued by later scholarship.

lessons.title: Launching the Cultural Revolution 1966-69
lessons.description: Big-character posters, Red Guards and the Four Olds — how Mao mobilised youth against the Party itself.
spec_references: China during the Cultural Revolution 1966-1976 — Reasons for the Cultural Revolution; impact on the people, including intellectuals and students; the role of the Red Guards
key_events_dates: Aug 1966 — Red Guards rally in Tiananmen Square
1968 — Down to the Countryside Movement begins
key_figures: Jiang Qing (Mao's wife, future Gang of Four)
Liu Shaoqi, purged and died in detention 1969
lessons.impartiality_notes: Present the Cultural Revolution as state-driven mass political violence; do not romanticise youth idealism while also not dismissing the genuine convictions of many participants.

lessons.title: Tibet, propaganda and the Mao cult
lessons.description: How the personality cult, struggle sessions and propaganda turned the Cultural Revolution into total state penetration.
spec_references: China during the Cultural Revolution — impact of Communism in Tibet; the nature of Communist propaganda and its impact, including Mao's personality cult; Dazhai community as a case study of Communist Party repression
key_events_dates: 1959 — Tibetan Uprising, Dalai Lama flees to India
1966-76 — Cultural Revolution destruction of Tibetan monasteries
1971 — Lin Biao dies fleeing in plane crash
lessons.impartiality_notes: Tibet is contested ground. State the PRC's 1950 incorporation as a fact and present both 'liberation' (PRC framing) and 'invasion/occupation' (Tibetan exile, many Western scholars) framings as held positions.

lessons.title: Mao's death, the Gang of Four and the Democracy Wall
lessons.description: Power struggle in 1976-78 — how Deng outmanoeuvred the Maoist left and reopened a sliver of debate.
spec_references: Communism in China after the death of Mao 1976-1981 — Attitudes to opposition and its repression after 1976, including the Gang of Four and the 'democracy wall'
key_events_dates: Dec 1978 — Third Plenum, Deng's reform line wins
key_figures: Gang of Four (Jiang Qing, Zhang Chunqiao, Yao Wenyuan, Wang Hongwen)
lessons.impartiality_notes: Present Wei Jingsheng's writings as historical evidence — not as proof of dissident heroism or as a footnote. Examiners want evidence-based judgement.

lessons.title: Deng's Four Modernisations and economic reform
lessons.description: Opening up, special economic zones and the household responsibility system — China after Mao.
spec_references: Communism in China after the death of Mao — changes in economic policy under Deng and its impact, including the Four Modernisations; the nature of Communist propaganda and its impact
key_events_dates: Dec 1978 — Four Modernisations adopted as official policy
1980 — First Special Economic Zones (Shenzhen, Zhuhai, Shantou, Xiamen)
1981 — Hua Guofeng resigns as Party Chairman
lessons.impartiality_notes: Frame economic reform as policy with winners and losers, not as unambiguous national success. Cite both growth statistics and regional inequality findings.

lessons.title: Women, education and the One Child Policy
lessons.description: How Deng's social policies reshaped families, schools and gender roles in the late 1970s and early 1980s.
spec_references: Communism in China after the death of Mao — social changes under Deng and its impact, including the role of women, changes in education and the One Child policy
key_figures: Song Jian, demographer behind One Child Policy
lessons.impartiality_notes: One Child Policy: present rationale (demographic-economic anxiety) alongside human-rights critiques (forced abortion, sex-selective abortion, ageing population). Avoid presenting either side as the official line.

article_units.name: Germany 1925-1955: The People and the State
article_units.subtitle: From Weimar to the Nazi state to a divided post-war Germany — thirty years of political extremes.
article_units.spec_section_focus: Non-British depth study, Component 1 Section B. 40 marks. Paired with International Relations 1918-1975.

lessons.title: The Weimar Republic 1925-1928
lessons.description: Stresemann's stabilisation — economic recovery, cultural flowering and the limits of Weimar democracy.
spec_references: The rise and consolidation of the Nazi regime 1925-1934 — Strengths and weaknesses of the Weimar Republic 1925-1928, including Nazi policies in the 1920s and the position of the party in 1928
lessons.impartiality_notes: Present the 'golden years' framing alongside structural problems (Article 48, proportional representation, agrarian discontent). Avoid retrospective inevitability.

lessons.title: The Depression and the rise of the Nazis 1929-1933
lessons.description: How mass unemployment, presidential government and elite miscalculation handed power to Hitler.
spec_references: The rise and consolidation of the Nazi regime — the impact of the Depression on different groups in Germany; the political, social and economic crisis of 1929-1933; rising support for Nazis 1929-1933
key_events_dates: Mar 1930 — Brüning becomes Chancellor, rule by decree
Sept 1930 — NSDAP wins 18.3% in Reichstag election
lessons.impartiality_notes: Frame Nazi rise as multi-causal: economic crisis, elite intrigue, Communist split on left, Nazi propaganda. Avoid 'Germans voted for the Holocaust' framing — the worst was not yet visible in 1932.

lessons.title: Consolidation of Nazi power 1933-1934
lessons.description: Reichstag Fire, Enabling Act, Night of the Long Knives — how Hitler turned chancellorship into dictatorship.
spec_references: The rise and consolidation of the Nazi regime — the Nazi consolidation of power 1933-1934, including the Reichstag Fire, the suspension of the Weimar constitution and the Enabling Act, the elections of March 1933, the takeover of/or collaboration with key institutions (particularly the army), and the elimination of opposition (including trade unions, opposition parties and the SA)
key_events_dates: Jul 1933 — Law against the Formation of New Parties
30 Jun 1934 — Night of the Long Knives
2 Aug 1934 — Hindenburg dies; Hitler becomes Führer; army oath
key_figures: Marinus van der Lubbe, Dutch communist charged with Reichstag Fire
Ernst Röhm, SA leader killed in purge
lessons.impartiality_notes: Reichstag Fire: present van der Lubbe verdict alongside historiographical debate over Nazi complicity (Tobias vs Mommsen). Do not assert as settled.

lessons.title: The Nazi terror state
lessons.description: Gestapo, SS, SD, courts — how a dictatorship combined repression with manufactured consent.
spec_references: Nazi Germany and its people 1933-1939 — Elements of the Nazi terror state, including the SA, SS, Gestapo, SD, courts and police
key_events_dates: Apr 1934 — Gestapo placed under SS control
Jun 1936 — Himmler appointed Chief of German Police
lessons.impartiality_notes: Cite revisionist scholarship (Robert Gellately, Eric Johnson) showing Gestapo relied heavily on civilian denunciations — terror was more participatory than the totalitarian model suggests.

lessons.title: Propaganda, culture and the cult of Hitler
lessons.description: Newsreels, rallies, radio and the Führer myth — how the regime built consent through mass communication.
spec_references: Nazi Germany and its people 1933-1939 — Nazi use of culture and propaganda; personal popularity of Hitler; attempts to create a National Community
key_events_dates: Mar 1933 — Reich Ministry of Public Enlightenment and Propaganda created
1938 — Volksempfänger radios in c.70% of households
lessons.impartiality_notes: Ian Kershaw's 'Hitler Myth' framing — that Hitler's personal popularity could outrun party policy — is mainstream and exam-relevant. Cite it.

lessons.title: Economy, society and the Nazi winners and losers
lessons.description: Rearmament, the Four-Year Plan, Strength Through Joy — and the workers, farmers and Mittelstand who paid for it.
spec_references: Nazi Germany and its people 1933-1939 — economic policies of Nazi regime and their effects on sections of German society (winners and losers); Nazi social policies, including policies on women and youth
key_events_dates: 1934-39 — German unemployment falls from ~6m to under 200,000
key_figures: Baldur von Schirach, Hitler Youth leader
lessons.impartiality_notes: Present unemployment statistics with caveat (women, Jews, conscripts removed from the count). Examiners reward students who can complicate the 'Nazi economic miracle' narrative.

lessons.title: Opposition, persecution and the racial state
lessons.description: From the Confessing Church to Kristallnacht — how the regime crushed dissent and escalated antisemitism.
spec_references: Nazi Germany and its people 1933-1939 — the lack of effective opposition to the regime; persecution of Jews and other groups, including Roma, Jehovah's Witnesses and homosexuals; eugenics policies
key_figures: Bishop Clemens von Galen, anti-T4 sermons (1941)
Herschel Grynszpan, whose action triggered Kristallnacht
lessons.impartiality_notes: Treat persecution of Roma, disabled people, homosexuals and Jehovah's Witnesses with the same factual specificity as antisemitic persecution. Examiner reports flag students who only know about Jews — losing marks for narrow coverage.

lessons.title: Germany at war 1939-1945
lessons.description: Initial victories, the Eastern Front, the Holocaust and total defeat — how the war ended Nazi Germany.
spec_references: War and its legacy 1939-1955 — Initial reaction to outbreak of war; changing fortunes of Germany in the war; growing impact of war, including bombing; extent of support for war effort; opposition during war; escalation of racial persecution leading to the Holocaust; defeat and occupation
key_figures: Hans and Sophie Scholl, White Rose (executed Feb 1943)
lessons.impartiality_notes: Treat Holocaust with documentary specificity (Wannsee, Einsatzgruppen, death camps). Do not abstract. Examiner reports note students confuse White Rose with Swing Movement and Edelweiss Pirates — drill named groups with named actions.

lessons.title: De-Nazification and divided Germany 1945-1955
lessons.description: Tribunals, rebuilding and the split into East and West — Germany under four-power occupation.
spec_references: War and its legacy 1939-1955 — Allied policy of de-Nazification (methods and impact); the differing experiences of people in East and West Germany 1945-1955
key_events_dates: 1955 — FRG joins NATO; GDR joins Warsaw Pact
lessons.impartiality_notes: Examiner reports specifically flag this topic (J410/02 Q6) as confusing students. Distinguish process (questionnaires, tribunals) from impact (statues removed, curricula rewritten, both Germanies eventually abandoning policy for economic recovery).

article_units.name: South Africa 1960-1994: The People and the State
article_units.subtitle: From Sharpeville to the first democratic election — resistance to apartheid and the negotiated end of a regime.
article_units.spec_section_focus: Non-British depth study, Component 1 Section B. 40 marks. Paired with International Relations 1918-1975.

lessons.title: Apartheid consolidation and the Bantustans
lessons.description: How Separate Development carved up South Africa — laws, homelands and the engineering of inequality.
spec_references: Opposition to the Apartheid regime c.1960s — The consolidation of Apartheid – Separate Development and the establishment of the Bantustans; nature and extent of support for Apartheid
key_events_dates: 1950 — Population Registration Act, Group Areas Act
lessons.impartiality_notes: Use the term apartheid as historical/legal terminology. Present the National Party's 'separate but equal' rhetoric as a stated rationale that was contradicted by every economic indicator. Cite scholarship (Saul Dubow, Hermann Giliomee).

lessons.title: Sharpeville and the turn to armed struggle
lessons.description: How the massacre of 21 March 1960 ended a half-century of peaceful protest and pushed the ANC underground.
spec_references: Opposition to the Apartheid regime c.1960s — the Sharpeville Massacre and its impact; reasons for, methods of and impact of different types of resistance, including the ANC, continuing impact of the Freedom Charter and Umkhonto we Sizwe and Poqo
lessons.impartiality_notes: MK's strategy was sabotage of property, not initially of people. State this accurately. Apartheid government framed all resistance as terrorism; present that framing as a contemporary political claim rather than a settled judgement.

lessons.title: Rivonia Trial and the long silence
lessons.description: Mandela's speech from the dock and the imprisonment of a generation of ANC leaders.
spec_references: Opposition to the Apartheid regime c.1960s — the Rivonia Trial 1964 and its consequences
key_events_dates: 20 Apr 1964 — Mandela 'I am prepared to die' speech
12 Jun 1964 — Eight defendants sentenced to life
lessons.impartiality_notes: Mandela was on the ANC and US terror watchlists until 2008. State this factually as evidence about how 'terrorism' is defined politically.
section_markers: I am prepared to die speech

lessons.title: Black Consciousness, Durban strikes and trade unions
lessons.description: Steve Biko, SASO and the labour militancy of the early 1970s — new fronts in the resistance.
spec_references: Growing resistance and repression c.1970s — The further development of resistance: the Black Consciousness Movement, SASO, women's groups, trade unions including the Durban workers' strike 1973
key_events_dates: 1973 — Federation of South African Trade Unions (FOSATU precursor)
lessons.impartiality_notes: Biko's death in police custody (Sept 1977) is documented in court inquest. State this factually rather than rhetorically.

lessons.title: Soweto Uprising and youth resistance
lessons.description: The Afrikaans-medium decree that brought schoolchildren onto the streets — and how the regime responded.
spec_references: Growing resistance and repression c.1970s — young people, including the Soweto students' uprising 1976; the ANC in exile
key_events_dates: 16 Jun 1976 — Soweto Uprising begins (Hector Pieterson killed)
Sept 1977 — Steve Biko dies in police custody
key_figures: Hector Pieterson, age 12, killed first day
lessons.impartiality_notes: Present 1976 death toll as state estimate vs Human Rights Commission estimate (~600-700). Note range.

lessons.title: International isolation and the Anti-Apartheid Movement
lessons.description: Sports boycotts, sanctions and divestment — how global pressure squeezed the apartheid economy.
spec_references: Growing resistance and repression c.1970s — the international Anti-Apartheid Movement; the impact of resistance on the Apartheid regime; the response of the regime to resistance
key_events_dates: 1985 — Chase Manhattan refuses to roll over loans
lessons.impartiality_notes: On Thatcher and Reagan's 'constructive engagement': present their stated rationale (sanctions hurt black South Africans most) alongside critics. Avoid editorialising on living/recent figures.

lessons.title: P.W. Botha's State of Emergency and total strategy
lessons.description: The UDF, township revolt and the regime's military response — apartheid at its most violent.
spec_references: The collapse of apartheid c.1980s-1994 — Growing pressure on the regime, including the impact of sanctions, the United Democratic Front, the growth and impact of mass resistance; the growth of Inkatha, 'civil war' and the impact on Black communities; opposition to the 1983 constitution; the State of Emergency 1985-1990
key_figures: Allan Boesak and Frank Chikane, UDF
lessons.impartiality_notes: Inkatha-ANC violence in KwaZulu-Natal and townships is contested ground. Truth and Reconciliation Commission documented state 'third force' involvement. State TRC findings as findings, not as final verdict.

lessons.title: Cuito Cuanavale, de Klerk and the negotiation begins
lessons.description: Military stalemate in Angola, factional split in the National Party and the unbanning of February 1990.
spec_references: The collapse of apartheid — divisions within the National Party government and the failure of 'total strategy', including the impact of the defeat at Cuito Cuanavale; the role of leading figures, including FW de Klerk, Ramaphosa and Mandela; negotiations between the government and the ANC; unbanning of the ANC, Pan African Congress and the South African Communist Party
key_events_dates: Aug 1989 — F.W. de Klerk replaces Botha
2 Feb 1990 — de Klerk unbans ANC, PAC, SACP
lessons.impartiality_notes: Present Cuito Cuanavale's military outcome as historically contested (both sides claimed victory). Cite Stephen Ellis, Vladimir Shubin, Piero Gleijeses for range of readings.

lessons.title: Election 1994 and the new South Africa
lessons.description: April 1994 — kilometre-long queues, ANC majority and Mandela's inauguration as post-apartheid president.
spec_references: The collapse of apartheid — the first free elections in 1994
key_events_dates: 27-29 Apr 1994 — South Africa's first non-racial general election
9 May 1994 — Mandela elected by National Assembly
key_figures: F.W. de Klerk, Deputy President under GNU
lessons.impartiality_notes: Frame 1994 as a negotiated settlement with compromises (sunset clauses, no land redistribution, civil service guarantees). Avoid 'Rainbow Nation' rhetoric uncritically.

article_units.name: The USA 1919-1948: The People and the State
article_units.subtitle: From the Roaring Twenties through the New Deal to the home front of the Second World War.
article_units.spec_section_focus: Non-British depth study, Component 1 Section B. 40 marks. Paired with International Relations 1918-1975.

lessons.title: The Roaring Twenties and Republican prosperity
lessons.description: Mass production, consumer credit and the boom that wasn't shared — who prospered and who didn't.
spec_references: The 'Roaring Twenties' — The US economy in the 'Roaring Twenties', including Republican party policies and ideology; areas of industry and social groups that did, and did not, experience prosperity
key_events_dates: 1920 — Warren Harding wins 'return to normalcy' election
1929 — US car production peaks at 5.6 million
lessons.impartiality_notes: Frame the decade as boom for some, hardship for others — farmers, African Americans, immigrants. Avoid a single-narrative 'jazz age' caricature.

lessons.title: Women, the Sheppard-Towner Act and the 19th Amendment
lessons.description: Suffrage won, flappers and feminism reframed — what the 19th Amendment did and did not change.
spec_references: The 'Roaring Twenties' — the US government and women in the 1920s, including women's rights movements and the Sheppard-Towner Act
key_figures: Carrie Chapman Catt, League of Women Voters
lessons.impartiality_notes: Note 19th Amendment did not enfranchise Black women in practice in the South due to Jim Crow voter suppression. State this factually.

lessons.title: Prohibition: causes, enforcement and failure
lessons.description: How the Volstead Act tried to dry out America — and what bootleggers, speakeasies and Al Capone did with it.
spec_references: The 'Roaring Twenties' — causes, aims, implementation and failure of prohibition
lessons.impartiality_notes: Present Prohibition's roots in Protestant temperance, Progressive reformism and anti-immigrant sentiment as the historical mix. Avoid simplifying as just 'religious bigotry'.

lessons.title: Jim Crow, the Klan and racial violence
lessons.description: Segregation in law, lynching in practice and the Klan's second revival — the 1920s as a decade of racial backlash.
spec_references: The 'Roaring Twenties' — prejudice and discrimination in US society, including the Jim Crow Laws and the Ku Klux Klan
key_events_dates: 1928 — Klan membership collapses after Stephenson scandal
lessons.impartiality_notes: Use 'Tulsa Race Massacre' rather than older 'riot' framing — Tulsa city government officially adopted 'massacre' in 2001. Cite findings of 2001 Oklahoma Commission.

lessons.title: Immigration, the Red Scare and nativism
lessons.description: Palmer Raids, Sacco and Vanzetti, the National Origins Act — how 1920s America closed its doors.
spec_references: The 'Roaring Twenties' — the Red Scare, including the Palmer Raids and Sacco and Vanzetti; restrictions on immigration throughout the 1920s; attempts to combat prejudice, including the NAACP and the UNIA
key_events_dates: 1916 onwards — UNIA growth under Marcus Garvey
key_figures: J. Edgar Hoover, head of GID then FBI
lessons.impartiality_notes: Sacco and Vanzetti's guilt has been debated for a century. Present trial as procedurally flawed (Massachusetts Governor Dukakis pardoned 1977) but do not assert innocence as fact.

lessons.title: The Great Depression and Hoover's response
lessons.description: Wall Street to bread lines — how the 1929 crash became the worst economic crisis in American history.
spec_references: The 1930s and the New Deal — Economic and social effects of the Great Depression and government response; Presidential election campaigns of 1932
key_events_dates: Jul 1932 — Bonus Army marches on Washington
lessons.impartiality_notes: Hoover did intervene (RFC, public works) — students often parrot 'Hoover did nothing'. Examiners want nuance: Hoover acted but inadequately by the scale of the crisis.

lessons.title: The First and Second New Deals
lessons.description: Hundred Days, Alphabet Agencies and the Wagner Act — Roosevelt's attempt to remake American government.
spec_references: The 1930s and the New Deal — Roosevelt and the First New Deal: the Hundred Days, Alphabet Agencies, including Agricultural Adjustment Agency, Civilian Conservation Corps, Federal Emergency Administration, National Recovery Administration and the Tennessee Valley Authority; the Second New Deal, including Works Progress Administration, Social Security Act, Wagner Act, Resettlement Administration and Farm Security Administration
lessons.impartiality_notes: Present the New Deal as politically contested at the time — from the left (Long, Townsend), the right (Liberty League), and the Supreme Court. Do not present it as a settled progressive triumph.

lessons.title: Reactions to the New Deal
lessons.description: Critics on left and right, Supreme Court reversals and the New Deal's limits for Black Americans.
spec_references: The 1930s and the New Deal — reactions to, and impact of, the New Deals
key_events_dates: 1935-36 — Supreme Court strikes down AAA, NRA
lessons.impartiality_notes: Highlight that New Deal agriculture and housing policies often excluded or hurt Black Americans (sharecropper displacement, redlining via FHA). Cite Ira Katznelson.

lessons.title: The Second World War and civil rights
lessons.description: Mobilisation, Japanese internment, Detroit riots and the wartime foundation of the civil rights movement.
spec_references: The impact of the Second World War on US society — The mobilisation of the US people for the war effort; increased government and Presidential powers; social impact of the war; women and the war effort; Japanese internment; the war as the foundation for the Civil Rights movement; the Detroit Race Riots 1943; segregation within the military; Executive Order 8802; desegregation of US troops in 1948
key_figures: A. Philip Randolph (March on Washington Movement)
lessons.impartiality_notes: Japanese internment: in 1988 Reagan signed Civil Liberties Act formally apologising. State this and the $20,000 reparations factually.

article_units.name: The USA 1945-1974: The People and the State
article_units.subtitle: The Red Scare, the civil rights movement and the radical decade — America from V-J Day to Nixon's resignation.
article_units.spec_section_focus: Non-British depth study, Component 1 Section B. 40 marks. Paired with International Relations 1918-1975.

lessons.title: The post-war Red Scare
lessons.description: Hoover, HUAC and the Rosenbergs — how Cold War anxiety reshaped American politics from 1947.
spec_references: Post-war challenges in the USA 1945-1954 — Concerns of US government about the influence of Communism in the USA and responses to these concerns, including media campaigns highlighting American values and institutions; the Red Scare of the late 1940s, including the role of J Edgar Hoover and the Rosenberg case
lessons.impartiality_notes: Examiner reports specifically note J Edgar Hoover (not Herbert Hoover the President). Drill this distinction. Rosenberg guilt: Venona decrypts (declassified 1995) confirm Julius's espionage; Ethel's role still debated.

lessons.title: McCarthyism
lessons.description: How a junior senator from Wisconsin made Communist subversion the dominant theme of US politics 1950-54.
spec_references: Post-war challenges in the USA — reaction to the Red Scare; the nature of, support for and opposition to McCarthyism
key_events_dates: 1953 — McCarthy becomes Senate Government Operations chair
lessons.impartiality_notes: Distinguish McCarthyism (Senate hearings, blacklists) from broader anti-Communism (which had bipartisan support). Both are mainstream historiographic positions.

lessons.title: African Americans before Brown v Board
lessons.description: Jim Crow in 1950s America — segregated schools, denied votes and the lawsuits that would change everything.
spec_references: Post-war challenges in the USA — the position of African Americans in US society, including the Jim Crow Laws, access to education, voting rights and lack of equality in employment
key_figures: Thurgood Marshall, NAACP Legal Defense Fund
lessons.impartiality_notes: Use specific Jim Crow examples (literacy tests, poll taxes, sundown towns) rather than generalised description. Examiners want concrete detail.

lessons.title: Brown, Montgomery and the early civil rights movement
lessons.description: Little Rock Nine, the Montgomery Bus Boycott and the rise of Martin Luther King Jr 1954-1960.
spec_references: Civil Rights in the USA 1954-1964 — The development and achievements of the civil rights movement, including Brown vs. Board of Education 1954; Montgomery Bus Boycott 1956; leadership of Martin Luther King in civil rights campaigns; roles of the SNCC, SCLC, NAACP in civil rights campaigns
key_events_dates: 1 Dec 1955 — Rosa Parks arrested; bus boycott begins
1956 — Browder v Gayle ends bus segregation
lessons.impartiality_notes: Rosa Parks was a trained NAACP activist, not just 'a tired seamstress'. Get this right — examiners reward complexity.

lessons.title: Freedom Rides to the Civil Rights Act 1964
lessons.description: Birmingham, March on Washington, Selma — how mass protest forced federal legislation.
spec_references: Civil Rights in the USA 1954-1964 — opposition to the civil rights movement, including illegal organisations and the police and state authorities; the contribution of government and official institutions in improving civil rights, including the roles of the Supreme Court in civil rights campaigns; the roles of Kennedy and Johnson in civil rights campaigns; reasons for, and impact of, the Civil Rights Act 1964
key_events_dates: Aug 1963 — March on Washington, 'I Have a Dream'
Jul 1964 — Civil Rights Act signed by LBJ
lessons.impartiality_notes: Kennedy's civil rights record was reluctant before 1963. Examiners want students who can distinguish symbolic Kennedy support from legislative LBJ delivery.

lessons.title: Malcolm X, Black Power and radical movements
lessons.description: From Nation of Islam to Black Panthers — Black radicalism alongside and against the King mainstream.
spec_references: Government and dissent c.1964-1974 — Development and impact of African American radical movements and leaders, including Malcolm X and Black Power
key_events_dates: Apr 1968 — Martin Luther King Jr assassinated
Oct 1968 — Olympic Black Power salute (Smith and Carlos)
lessons.impartiality_notes: Black Panthers ran free breakfast programmes, medical clinics — not only armed patrols. Present both dimensions. Cite COINTELPRO documents (declassified Church Committee 1975) on FBI surveillance.

lessons.title: Native Americans, Chicanos and other civil rights movements
lessons.description: AIM, the UFW, Wounded Knee and Cesar Chavez — civil rights beyond Black-and-white America.
spec_references: Government and dissent c.1964-1974 — impact of civil rights campaigns for Native Americans and Chicanos
lessons.impartiality_notes: Wounded Knee 1973: present the 71-day occupation factually. AIM's relationship with FBI is documented and contested — cite the Church Committee findings.

lessons.title: Feminism and the women's movement
lessons.description: Betty Friedan, NOW, the ERA fight and the Stonewall riots — gender and sexuality politics in the 1960s and 1970s.
spec_references: Government and dissent c.1964-1974 — development of feminist movements, including Betty Friedan and National Organisation for Women; the impact of feminism, including Status Commission 1963, Equal Pay Act, use of Civil Rights Act, the 1972 Supreme Court ruling on equal rights; Stonewall riots 1969
key_events_dates: 1961 — President's Commission on the Status of Women
1972 — Equal Rights Amendment passed by Congress
lessons.impartiality_notes: ERA failed ratification despite congressional passage. Present Schlafly's STOP ERA campaign as a major historical force, not a footnote — politically impartial teaching requires showing why opposition succeeded.

lessons.title: Vietnam protests, Great Society and Nixon's America
lessons.description: Anti-war movement, LBJ's domestic agenda and Nixon's pledges — political divisions on the road to Watergate.
spec_references: Government and dissent c.1964-1974 — political, economic and social divisions in the USA: anti-Vietnam War protests, campaigns to improve welfare of the poor, Johnson's 'Great Society', Nixon's pledges on welfare
key_events_dates: 1964-65 — Great Society legislation: Medicare, Medicaid, ESEA, Voting Rights Act
lessons.impartiality_notes: On Nixon: stick to documented record (Family Assistance Plan, EPA, Title IX expansion alongside Watergate, anti-war repression). Don't editorialise on motives.

article_units.name: Migration to Britain c.1000-c.2010
article_units.subtitle: A thousand years of arrivals, communities and identity in Britain — Jewish, Huguenot, Irish, Caribbean, South Asian, EU.
article_units.spec_section_focus: Thematic study, Component 2. 50 marks. Must be taken with Impact of Empire + Spitalfields. Developed with BASA.

lessons.title: England before 1066 and the Norman impact on migration
lessons.description: Diversity in late Anglo-Saxon England, the Norman conquest as elite migration and resistance to it.
spec_references: c.1000-1500 — Population diversity in England before 1066; the impact of the Norman Conquest; resistance to the Normans in William's reign
key_events_dates: Pre-1066 — Scandinavian-descended populations in north and east
lessons.impartiality_notes: Frame the Norman Conquest as both conquest and (in narrow elite terms) migration. Avoid presenting it solely as 'invasion'.

lessons.title: Jews in medieval England 1066-1290
lessons.description: Arrival with the Normans, blood libels, royal taxation and Edward I's expulsion of 1290.
spec_references: c.1000-1500 — Jews in England: their first arrival in 1066 and their treatment and experiences until their expulsion in 1290
key_events_dates: 1066 — Jewish merchants arrive with William I
1218 — Jews required to wear identifying badge
lessons.impartiality_notes: Use 'blood libel' as the historical term for the antisemitic accusation. State that it was false and that medieval English authorities (Henry III) at points debunked it.

lessons.title: Africans, Asians and other migrants in early modern England
lessons.description: Tudor Africans, the East India Company and the arrival of South Asian seafarers in the 1600s.
spec_references: c.1000-1500 — Immigrants in England during the Middle Ages: the lives and impact of resident 'aliens'
c.1500-1900 — Africans in sixteenth century England: reasons for their arrival; their experiences
c.1500-1900 — The foundation of the East India Company and arrivals from the Indian subcontinent — Lascar and other Asian merchant seamen, child servants and ayahs
key_events_dates: 1501 — Catherine of Aragon's retinue includes African attendants
1555 — John Lok brings five Africans to London
1660s onwards — Lascar seamen arrive in London
key_figures: John Blanke, royal trumpeter (Henry VIII court)
lessons.impartiality_notes: Cite Miranda Kaufmann's Black Tudors and Onyeka Nubia. Avoid both 'Tudor England was diverse' as celebratory anachronism and 'Africans were always enslaved' as flattening simplification.

lessons.title: Jewish readmission and Huguenot refugees
lessons.description: Cromwell's 1656 reopening, the Huguenots' Protestant exile and the Palatines of 1709.
spec_references: c.1500-1900 — The readmission of Jews in 1656 and their experiences; religious refugees – the arrival of Protestant refugees from the 1670s including the Huguenots and the Palatines
key_events_dates: 1656 — Cromwell allows Jewish readmission de facto
1685 — Edict of Fontainebleau (Huguenot expulsion from France)
key_figures: Menasseh ben Israel, rabbi who lobbied Cromwell
lessons.impartiality_notes: Frame the Huguenot reception as the canonical 'good refugee' narrative in British history — but note resentment in silk-weaving trade also existed.

lessons.title: Atlantic slavery and British ports
lessons.description: Royal African Company, Bristol-Liverpool-London, racial hierarchy and Black communities in 18th-century Britain.
spec_references: c.1500-1900 — The growth of African communities in Britain: reasons including the Royal African Company and the trade in enslaved Africans, loss of the American colonies and the expansion of the British Empire
lessons.impartiality_notes: Use 'enslaved African' / 'enslaved person' rather than 'slave' where it refers to a person (matches updated Pearson 2026 guidance and BASA conventions). 'Slave trade' as historical term remains.

lessons.title: Industrial Britain: Irish, Scottish and Eastern European migrants
lessons.description: Irish famine migrants, Eastern European Jewish refugees and Britain's first immigration controls.
spec_references: c.1500-1900 — Impact of the Industrial Revolution on migration: Irish and Scottish migrants to England; the impact of migrants on political movements including the Abolition movement and the Chartists; Eastern European Jewish immigrants, their experiences and impact; The process of naturalisation and denization: government legislation on immigration and nationality, including the Naturalisation Act of 1870
key_events_dates: 1881-1914 — c.150,000 Eastern European Jews settle in Britain
key_figures: Sir William Vernon Harcourt, Home Secretary 1880s
lessons.impartiality_notes: Frame the 1905 Aliens Act as Britain's first peacetime immigration control — directed primarily at Eastern European Jewish refugees. State this factually.

lessons.title: Two world wars and inter-war migration
lessons.description: Belgian refugees, the Aliens Acts, the Jewish refugee crisis of the 1930s and Polish settlement after 1945.
spec_references: 1900-c.2010 — The continued growth of diverse port communities in the early twentieth century; Government legislation in the first half of the twentieth century: the reasons for, and impact of, the Aliens Act 1905, the Status of Aliens Act 1914 and the British Nationality Act 1948; The arrival of Jewish refugees in the 1930s; different attitudes towards Jews in Britain in the 1930s; the experiences of migrants and their descendants during the two world wars; the experience of Poles who settled in Britain after the Second World War
key_events_dates: 1919 — Race riots in Cardiff, Liverpool, South Shields
lessons.impartiality_notes: 1930s British attitudes to Jewish refugees were mixed — refusal of visas to many German Jews is documented. State this without uncritical celebration of Kindertransport.

lessons.title: Commonwealth migration after 1945
lessons.description: Windrush, Caribbean nurses, South Asian Britons and the political backlash that produced Enoch Powell.
spec_references: 1900-c.2010 — Commonwealth migration after the Second World War: the varied reasons for this immigration; the impact of immigrants; the experiences of immigrants; the resulting debate over immigration – political racism and antiracism; the impact of race relations legislation and immigration controls including the 1962 Commonwealth Immigrants Act
key_events_dates: 1948 — British Nationality Act; HMT Empire Windrush arrives
1972 — Ugandan Asians expelled by Idi Amin, ~28,000 admitted to UK
key_figures: Sam King, Windrush passenger and Mayor of Southwark
Claudia Jones, Notting Hill Carnival founder
lessons.impartiality_notes: Enoch Powell's 1968 speech is a defining moment. Quote sparingly from primary text; analyse rather than dramatise. Cite Trevor Phillips and David Olusoga for range of subsequent analysis.

lessons.title: Multicultural Britain 1981-2010
lessons.description: 1981 British Nationality Act, asylum seekers, EU enlargement and the political shift on immigration after 1990.
spec_references: 1900-c.2010 — the 1981 British Nationality Act; Immigration as a political issue c.1990-c.2010: the debate over a 'multi-cultural society'; attitudes towards, and treatment of, political refugees and asylum seekers; the issues raised by EU 'open borders'
lessons.impartiality_notes: Stephen Lawrence and Macpherson Report's finding of 'institutional racism' is documented government finding. State as such. EU enlargement: present both 'free movement was a benefit' and 'free movement was disruptive' as live political positions.

lessons.title: Ideas of Englishness and Britishness over time
lessons.description: How British identity has been defined, redefined and contested from 1500 to 2010.
spec_references: c.1500-1900 — (from c.1500) Ideas of national 'identity' – how we have differently defined 'Englishness' and 'Britishness' over time
1900-c.2010 — Ideas of national 'identity'
key_events_dates: 2002 — Life in the UK test introduced
key_figures: Linda Colley, historian of British identity
lessons.impartiality_notes: Final lesson is partly historiographic. Present Britishness as historically constructed and contested. Cite Linda Colley's Britons.

article_units.name: Power: Monarchy and Democracy in Britain c.1000-2014
article_units.subtitle: A thousand-year story of who ruled Britain — Anglo-Saxon kings, medieval barons, Tudors, Parliament, the people.
article_units.spec_section_focus: Thematic study, Component 2. 50 marks. Must be taken with English Reformation + Kenilworth.

lessons.title: Anglo-Saxon kingship c.1000-1066
lessons.description: Witan, thegns and the king's peace — how power worked before the Norman Conquest.
spec_references: c.1000-c.1485 — Anglo-Saxon kingship c.1000-1066: the basis of kingship; the power and responsibilities of the kings; relations between the kings and the thegns
key_events_dates: c.1000 — Æthelred II rules a unified English kingdom
5 Jan 1066 — Edward dies; Harold Godwinson crowned
1066 — Three claimants: Harold, William of Normandy, Harald Hardrada
lessons.impartiality_notes: Use the term 'Witan' as the historical body advising the king. Avoid anachronistic 'parliament-like' framing.

lessons.title: The Norman monarchy and feudal power 1066-1154
lessons.description: Tenants-in-chief, Domesday and the great barons — how William and his successors held England.
spec_references: c.1000-c.1485 — Different claims to the throne in 1066: the Norman invasion, including the establishment of the Norman monarchy and the transfer of power from Saxons to Normans at all levels of society; the extent of the power of the monarch and the barons by 1087
lessons.impartiality_notes: Domesday is a primary source — present it as evidence with limitations (rural focus, incomplete coverage).

lessons.title: Magna Carta and the emergence of Parliament 1199-1399
lessons.description: King John, Simon de Montfort, Edward I and the slow birth of a representative assembly.
spec_references: c.1000-c.1485 — Struggles over power: John's ascension and early revolts against his rule; John and Magna Carta; emergence of Parliament in the reigns of Henry III and Edward I, including the role and importance of Simon de Montfort; deposition of Richard II in 1399; Wars of the Roses
key_events_dates: Jan 1265 — Simon de Montfort's Parliament (first with commoners)
Aug 1265 — Battle of Evesham, de Montfort killed
lessons.impartiality_notes: Examiner reports flag confusion between John and Charles I. Drill the distinction. John's grievances were taxation and military failure (Normandy), not 'ship money' — that's Charles I.

lessons.title: Tudor monarchy and Parliament
lessons.description: Henry VIII's break with Rome through Parliament, and Elizabeth I's management of religion, finance and succession.
spec_references: c.1485-c.1800 — Tudor government: growth of royal power under Henry VIII; the role of Parliament under Henry VIII and Elizabeth I
lessons.impartiality_notes: Examiner reports (J410/09 2022 Q1) note students confuse Charles I's parliamentary disputes with Tudor ones. Keep the period boundary strict.

lessons.title: Civil War, Republic and Restoration
lessons.description: Charles I's personal rule, the abolition of monarchy and Charles II's return — Parliament becomes indispensable.
spec_references: c.1485-c.1800 — Defeat and return of monarchy: Charles I's personal rule 1629-1640; the Civil Wars and the abolition of the monarchy; the Restoration of the monarchy in 1660
lessons.impartiality_notes: Pair this lesson with the British depth study unit (Personal Rule to Restoration) if students take that combination — content overlaps and reinforces.

lessons.title: The Glorious Revolution and parliamentary monarchy
lessons.description: 1688, the Bill of Rights and the slow consolidation of parliamentary sovereignty in the 18th century.
spec_references: c.1485-c.1800 — James II's rule and the reasons for the 1688 Revolution (The Glorious Revolution); the legacy of the Glorious Revolution including the Bill of Rights; the development of Parliament under William III and Anne; the emergence of political parties and the development of a Parliamentary monarchy in the course of the 1700s
lessons.impartiality_notes: 'Glorious Revolution' was glorious primarily for Anglican Protestants. The Catholic-Jacobite perspective is part of the historical record — pair with the J410/11 unit for fuller picture.

lessons.title: Reform Acts and the expansion of the franchise 1832-1928
lessons.description: Great Reform Act, working-class enfranchisement and the long struggle for votes for women.
spec_references: c.1800-2014 — The changing relationship between Parliament and people c.1800 to c.1918: dissatisfaction with electoral system by early 1800s; reasons for and impacts of the Parliamentary Reform Acts of 1832, 1867 and 1884; the rise and effectiveness of mass Trade Unions and the Labour Party 1880s-1914; the struggle for the vote for women and the reasons why it was won for some women in 1918
lessons.impartiality_notes: Examiner reports (J410/09 2022 Q1) explicitly warn against using Suffragettes (WSPU) interchangeably with Suffragists (NUWSS) — drill the distinction.

lessons.title: State, war and welfare 1914-1979
lessons.description: Two world wars expanded state power and built the welfare state — from DORA to the NHS to nationalisation.
spec_references: c.1800-2014 — The changing relationship between Parliament and people c.1914-c.1980: government control in the world wars; the increased role of the state from 1945 to c.1980
lessons.impartiality_notes: Frame the welfare state as a cross-party post-war settlement, not solely a Labour achievement (the 1944 Education Act was Conservative; 1942 Beveridge was a Liberal report).

lessons.title: Pressure groups, Thatcher and challenges to Parliament
lessons.description: CND, Greenpeace, Miners' Strike — how organised non-party pressure reshaped politics.
spec_references: c.1800-2014 — Challenges to Parliament c.1980 to early 2000s: the Miners' Strike 1984-1985, CND and Greenpeace; Prime Ministerial power under Thatcher and Blair
lessons.impartiality_notes: Examiner reports (J410/09 2022 Q3) note students use pressure groups from the wrong period. Stick to the named groups in the spec.

lessons.title: Devolution and coalition government
lessons.description: Scottish and Welsh devolution, the 2010 coalition and the question of where power now lies.
spec_references: c.1800-2014 — the devolution of power to regions of the UK; the challenges of coalition government
key_events_dates: 1997 — Devolution referendums in Scotland and Wales
1999 — Scottish Parliament and Welsh Assembly open
lessons.impartiality_notes: Devolution and Scottish independence are politically live questions. Present the 1997 referendum and 2014 vote as facts with cited turnouts and margins; avoid editorial framing.

article_units.name: War and British Society c.790-c.2010
article_units.subtitle: Vikings to Iraq — how a thousand years of warfare reshaped British people, politics and the state.
article_units.spec_section_focus: Thematic study, Component 2. 50 marks. Must be taken with Personal Rule to Restoration + Kenilworth.

lessons.title: Viking raids on Anglo-Saxon England 790-1066
lessons.description: Lindisfarne to Stamford Bridge — how Scandinavian raiding and settlement transformed Anglo-Saxon society.
spec_references: c.790-c.1500 — Viking raids on Anglo-Saxon England 790-1066: impact of the raids; responses to the raids
key_events_dates: 878 — Battle of Edington, Treaty of Wedmore
lessons.impartiality_notes: Use 'Viking' as the conventional historical term; note distinction between raiders, traders and settlers.

lessons.title: Norman conquest and feudal warfare 1066-1215
lessons.description: Hastings, castle-building, the feudal levy and the breakdown of feudal order under Stephen and John.
spec_references: c.790-c.1500 — The Norman Conquest: English resistance; the establishment of Norman control under William I; the establishment of the Feudal system; the extent of the impact of the changes introduced by the Normans on different levels of society; Feudal society c.1100-1215: feudal relationship between monarchs and barons; breakdowns in the relationship under Stephen 1135-1154 and John 1214-1216
lessons.impartiality_notes: Connect this lesson to Kenilworth Castle (the historic environment site) — castles as instruments of Norman conquest.

lessons.title: Late medieval warfare c.1290-c.1450
lessons.description: Edward I's Welsh and Scottish wars, the Hundred Years' War and the cost of professional armies.
spec_references: c.790-c.1500 — Significance of war in medieval society c.1290-c.1450: changing nature of war and its effects; development and adaptation of feudal service; financial cost of war; impact on populations where armies fought or were stationed
lessons.impartiality_notes: Welsh and Scottish wars: use 'Edward I's conquest' as historical term. Welsh and Scottish perspectives on these wars differ from English ones — note this.

lessons.title: Elizabeth, Spain and the new world
lessons.description: Privateers, the Armada and the impact of Tudor maritime warfare on English society and the Crown.
spec_references: c.1500-c.1750 — Elizabeth I's wars with Spain in Europe and in the new world, their impact on the prestige and power of the monarch and relations with Parliament; the actions of English privateers, including their impact on the security, economy and the people of England
lessons.impartiality_notes: Privateers and slave-trading: Hawkins is documented as an early English slave-trader. State factually; do not romanticise as 'sea dogs'.

lessons.title: Border warfare c.1500-c.1600
lessons.description: Reivers, raids and the rough business of policing the Anglo-Scottish frontier.
spec_references: c.1500-c.1750 — Warfare on the English-Scottish borders and its impact on border society c.1500-c.1600
key_events_dates: 1600s — End of formal Border Reiver activity
lessons.impartiality_notes: Border Reivers operated as both Scottish and English subjects depending on raid direction. State factually.

lessons.title: Civil Wars in England, Scotland and Ireland 1642-1651
lessons.description: The Wars of the Three Kingdoms — Marston Moor, Naseby, Drogheda and the cost of civil war.
spec_references: c.1500-c.1750 — The Civil Wars of 1642-1651 in England, Scotland and Ireland: the nature of these wars; their impact on the people of England, Scotland and Ireland
key_events_dates: 1649 — Charles I executed; Cromwell's Irish campaign (Drogheda, Wexford)
lessons.impartiality_notes: Drogheda 1649 and Wexford: Cromwell's campaigns. State documented death tolls (c.3,500 at Drogheda) and contemporary debate over whether laws of war were broken. Sensitive in Irish historical memory.

lessons.title: Jacobite rebellions and imperial wars
lessons.description: The '15, the '45, Culloden and the Seven Years War — Britain's wars at home and around the world.
spec_references: c.1500-c.1750 — The Jacobite Wars 1715 and 1745: the impact on Scotland of the repression of the Jacobites; Imperial wars in the 18th and early 19th centuries: gains made in Seven Years War (1756-1763) and their effects on Britain
key_events_dates: 1745-46 — Jacobite Rising; Battle of Culloden Apr 1746
1759 — Battle of the Plains of Abraham (Quebec)
lessons.impartiality_notes: Highland Clearances are politically sensitive in Scottish memory. State documented facts (Disarming Act 1746, Heritable Jurisdictions Act 1747); avoid romanticised either pro- or anti-Jacobite framing.

lessons.title: Napoleonic wars and Victorian imperial conflicts
lessons.description: Trafalgar, Waterloo, Crimea, the Boer Wars — how war shaped 19th-century Britain.
spec_references: c.1750-c.2010 — Wars against Revolutionary / Napoleonic France and subsequent effects on British society and politics; Imperial conflicts in the second half of the 19th century: effects of the Crimean War; Boer Wars 1880-1881 and 1899-1902
key_events_dates: 1854 — Charge of the Light Brigade; Florence Nightingale at Scutari
lessons.impartiality_notes: Second Boer War concentration camps: documented and acknowledged. State factually. Boer perspective and Black African civilian deaths in camps both part of historical record.

lessons.title: Two world wars and total war 1914-1945
lessons.description: Conscription, rationing, the Home Front and how 'total war' transformed the relationship between state and citizen.
spec_references: c.1750-c.2010 — The First and Second World Wars: the beginnings of 'total war', including the impact on people's lives, increased state power and the changing relationship between the state and the people
key_events_dates: 1914-18 — First World War; British military deaths ~750,000
1939-45 — Second World War; British military deaths ~384,000, civilian ~70,000
lessons.impartiality_notes: Strategic bombing in WWII (Dresden, Hamburg) is a contested moral question in history. State documented death tolls; cite range of historians (Frederick Taylor, A.C. Grayling).

lessons.title: Cold War, IRA and the wars on terror
lessons.description: From CND to 7/7 — how post-1945 conflict shaped British politics, security and civil liberty.
spec_references: c.1750-c.2010 — Post-1945 conflicts - impacts and popular responses: Cold War and Britain in the 1950s and 1960s; IRA campaigns 1969-1994; the Iraq War 2003; terrorist threats and counter measures post-2003
key_events_dates: 2003 — Iraq War begins; 15 Feb 2003 Stop the War march (London ~1m)
lessons.impartiality_notes: Iraq War 2003 is contested ground. Cite Chilcot Report (2016) findings as the documented inquiry conclusion. Do not editorialise. Northern Ireland: avoid favouring either republican or unionist framing — use Good Friday Agreement language ('communities', 'consent') where possible.

article_units.name: Impact of Empire on Britain 1688-c.1730 with Spitalfields
article_units.subtitle: Glorious Revolution to South Sea Bubble — Britain's leap to global power, plus the migrant story of Spitalfields.
article_units.spec_section_focus: British depth study + historic environment, Component 3. 55 marks total (depth 35 + historic environment 20). Paired with Migration thematic study. Spitalfields is the fixed urban environment site from 2020 onwards. Developed with BASA.

lessons.title: Glorious Revolution and the Hanoverian succession
lessons.description: 1688, the Bill of Rights and how a Protestant monarchy reshaped British power at home and abroad.
spec_references: English expansion and its impact on the British Isles c.1688-c.1730 — Significance of the Glorious Revolution and the Hanoverian succession on England's position within the British Isles
key_events_dates: Nov 1688 — William of Orange lands at Brixham
Feb 1689 — William III and Mary II crowned jointly
lessons.impartiality_notes: 'Glorious Revolution' celebrates a Protestant Whig outcome — present Jacobite/Catholic perspective as historical reality, not heresy.

lessons.title: Ireland 1688-1691 and the Jacobite threat
lessons.description: Boyne, Aughrim and the Penal Laws — how William's victory reshaped Anglo-Irish society.
spec_references: English expansion — military campaigns in Ireland 1688-1691 and the settlement which followed
lessons.impartiality_notes: Highly contested in Irish memory (Battle of the Boyne is annually commemorated by Loyal Orders). State facts plainly; avoid celebratory or condemnatory framing.

lessons.title: Scotland 1688-1715: Glencoe to Union
lessons.description: Massacre at Glencoe, the failed Darien Scheme and the Act of Union 1707.
spec_references: English expansion — relationship between England and Scotland after 1688 including Jacobite opposition and the Massacre of Glencoe 1692; Darien Scheme and the Act of Union 1707; Jacobite Rebellion 1715
lessons.impartiality_notes: Glencoe and the Union of 1707 are politically resonant in modern Scottish debate. Stick to documented record.

lessons.title: Emigration from the British Isles
lessons.description: Voluntary, indentured and forced emigration to the Americas — who left, why and what they faced.
spec_references: English expansion — Emigration (including forced emigration) from the British Isles to the Americas
key_events_dates: 1700s — Scots and Ulster Scots emigrate to American colonies
lessons.impartiality_notes: Distinguish indentured servitude (time-limited contract) from chattel slavery (lifelong, heritable). Use precise terminology.

lessons.title: Bank of England, East India Company and the trade revolution
lessons.description: Financial revolution, Mughal trade and the establishment of Britain's commercial empire.
spec_references: Economic impact of empire on Britain 1688-c.1730 — Economic impact of war and imperial expansion: changes to the British economy; establishment of the Bank of England (1694); growing trade with India and China and the establishment in Kolkata and role of the East India Company
lessons.impartiality_notes: EIC operated in partnership with Mughal political authority initially. State factually rather than as 'British rule of India' anachronism.

lessons.title: Royal African Company and the slave economy
lessons.description: How the lifting of the RAC monopoly opened up British slave trading and reshaped Atlantic commerce.
spec_references: Economic impact of empire — political and economic impact of the lifting of the Royal African Company monopoly 1698; Treaty of Utrecht 1713; the South Sea Bubble 1719; economic importance of colonies in North America and Caribbean; origins and development of the slave based economy
lessons.impartiality_notes: Use 'enslaved African' / 'enslaved person'. Frame economic data alongside the human reality. Cite documented mortality on Middle Passage.

lessons.title: Consumerism, coffee houses and political activism
lessons.description: Sugar, tea and coffee — how empire transformed daily life, public debate and the politics of slavery.
spec_references: Political and social impact of empire on Britain 1688-c.1730 — The emergence of consumerism and its wider political and economic impacts; involvement of the British population in the slave trade including: the development of 'slave ports' – Bristol, Liverpool, London – and involvement of smaller ports; growth of ideas of a racial hierarchy and impact of these ideas on settled minority communities; opposition to slavery and the slave trade (including slave resistance); developing political activism including the role of coffee houses
key_events_dates: 1701 — Trial of Quobna Ottobah Cugoano context
1710s — Bristol overtakes London in slave voyages
lessons.impartiality_notes: Frame the rise of racial hierarchy as a historical phenomenon with documented contemporaries who opposed it (Quakers, individual writers). Cite scholarship (David Olusoga, Catherine Hall).

lessons.title: Spitalfields: site introduction and Huguenot weavers
lessons.description: Why Spitalfields became a refugee silk-weaving district — the Huguenot foundation of a migrant neighbourhood.
spec_references: Urban Environments: Patterns of Migration — when immigrant groups arrived, why and from where; the experiences of immigrants, including daily lives and occupations; the impact of migration on the area (Spitalfields fixed site from 2020)
