key_events_dates: 1685 — Edict of Fontainebleau expels French Huguenots
lessons.impartiality_notes: Site-specific factual lesson. Examiner reports for Section B reward integration of source comparison (e.g. Huguenot Hospital records, weaver portraits, surviving architecture).

lessons.title: Spitalfields: Irish, Jewish and Bangladeshi communities
lessons.description: Successive waves of arrival — Irish dockers, Jewish refugees from Tsarist Russia and Bangladeshi migrants.
spec_references: Urban Environments: Patterns of Migration — how immigrants were received by settled populations; key events in local migration history; the impact of migration on the area
key_events_dates: 1810s — Irish settle in Spitalfields after Famine pressure
1976 — Brick Lane Jamme Masjid converted from synagogue
lessons.impartiality_notes: Brick Lane Jamme Masjid building's three uses (Huguenot chapel 1743, synagogue 1898, mosque 1976) is the most exam-relevant single architectural symbol in Spitalfields. Drill it. Battle of Cable Street is exam-anchored — present documented turnout (c.100,000 anti-fascists).

lessons.title: Source skills for Spitalfields and Empire
lessons.description: How to use buildings, parish registers, newspapers and oral history as evidence for the historic environment paper.
spec_references: Urban Environments: Patterns of Migration — Sites may provide evidence about patterns of migration in a number of ways; how the site is presented and described in accompanying material
key_events_dates: Spitalfields parish registers (Christ Church): documented from 1729
Jewish East End oral histories (BBC, late 20th century)
Bangladeshi community oral histories (Tower Hamlets Local History Library)
key_figures: Tower Hamlets Local History Library and Archives
lessons.impartiality_notes: This lesson is technique-focused. Drill the 10-mark source comparison structure (integrated comparison, contextual knowledge anchored to site) per examiner expectations.

article_units.name: The English Reformation c.1520-c.1550 with Kenilworth Castle
article_units.subtitle: Henry VIII's break with Rome, the dissolution of the monasteries and Edwardian Protestantism — plus Kenilworth Castle as historic environment.
article_units.spec_section_focus: British depth study + historic environment, Component 3. 55 marks total. Paired with Power thematic study. Kenilworth Castle is the fixed site from 2019 onwards.

lessons.title: The pre-Reformation English Church c.1520
lessons.description: Parish life, monasteries and the place of the Church in ordinary lives before Henry's break with Rome.
spec_references: English Reformation c.1520-c.1535 — Role and importance (including wealth) of the church in England c.1520; religious practice and the relationship between the church and ordinary people
key_events_dates: 1520 — Church owns ~20% of land in England
c.1520 — c.825 monastic houses in England
1521 — Henry VIII receives 'Defender of the Faith' title
lessons.impartiality_notes: Cite Eamon Duffy's Stripping of the Altars for the 'vibrant late-medieval Catholicism' historiographic position alongside older 'corrupt church' framings.

lessons.title: Lollards, Luther and English criticism of the church
lessons.description: How Wycliffe's Lollards and Luther's 1517 theses prepared the intellectual ground for English Protestantism.
spec_references: English Reformation c.1520-c.1535 — the role and impact of the Lollards' and Luther's ideas; critics of the English church in the 1530s; popular attitudes towards reform of the church
key_events_dates: 1521 — Luther's books burned at Paul's Cross
1525 — Tyndale's English New Testament printed in Worms
lessons.impartiality_notes: Treat Catholic and Protestant theological positions as positions, not as 'right' and 'wrong'. Examiner reports reward students who can articulate both.

lessons.title: The King's Great Matter and the Reformation Parliament
lessons.description: Henry VIII's annulment, Cromwell's legislative revolution and the break with Rome 1529-1534.
spec_references: English Reformation c.1520-c.1535 — Henry VIII's desire to annul his first marriage; the legislation of the Reformation Parliament 1529-1534
key_events_dates: 1533 — Act in Restraint of Appeals; Cranmer annuls marriage to Catherine; Anne Boleyn married
lessons.impartiality_notes: Spec is clear: students do NOT need international political context (Charles V, Pope Clement VII) beyond background. Don't over-teach. Focus on legislation and its impact.

lessons.title: Valor Ecclesiasticus and Visitation of the Monasteries
lessons.description: How Cromwell's surveyors built the case for dissolution by counting monastic wealth and 'sin'.
spec_references: Dissolution of the Monasteries c.1534-c.1540 — Thomas Cromwell and the Valor Ecclesiasticus; the Visitation of the Monasteries; the process of dissolution
lessons.impartiality_notes: Visitors' findings were politically motivated. Present them as state-collected evidence whose reliability historians debate (G.W. Bernard, J.J. Scarisbrick).

lessons.title: Dissolution: process, impact and resistance
lessons.description: Suppression Acts, monks pensioned and the Pilgrimage of Grace — how the great monasteries fell.
spec_references: Dissolution of the Monasteries — Suppression Acts 1536 and 1539; immediate reactions to Dissolution including support, those who took advantage and those who opposed; effects of Dissolution on religious orders; effects on lives of ordinary people, especially the old and poor; cultural impacts; resistance and protest, including the Lincolnshire Rising and the Pilgrimage of Grace 1536-1537
key_events_dates: 1540 — Glastonbury Abbey suppressed; Abbot Whiting executed
key_figures: Robert Aske, Pilgrimage of Grace leader
lessons.impartiality_notes: Pilgrimage of Grace was the largest English rebellion of the century. Present its motivations (religious, economic, political) without flattening into one cause. Cite R.W. Hoyle.

lessons.title: Religious worship under Henry and Edward
lessons.description: Ten Articles, Six Articles, English Bible, Book of Common Prayer — the shifting religious settlement 1536-1552.
spec_references: The impact of the Reformation in English parishes c.1534-c.1550 — Development and changes in religious policy under Henry VIII and Edward VI; effects on religious worship, including church services, prayer books and the issue of the Bible in English; impact on the fabric of churches; effects on the clergy
key_events_dates: 1539 — Act of Six Articles (Catholic doctrine reaffirmed)
1552 — Book of Common Prayer (second edition, more Protestant)
lessons.impartiality_notes: Edward VI's regents had their own theological agendas distinct from Henry's. Cite Diarmaid MacCulloch for clear narrative.

lessons.title: Parish reaction and the Prayer Book Rebellion
lessons.description: How ordinary parishioners experienced the Reformation — and how Devon and Cornwall rebelled in 1549.
spec_references: The impact of the Reformation in English parishes — response of ordinary people to religious changes; resistance and protest, including the Prayer Book Rebellion 1549; enforcement of new religious policies
lessons.impartiality_notes: Western Rebellion's grievance was loss of Latin mass — present rebel demands from documented Articles. Cite Diarmaid MacCulloch and Eamon Duffy.

lessons.title: Kenilworth Castle: location and physical fabric
lessons.description: Why Kenilworth stands where it does — strategic Warwickshire site and what its stone reveals about power.
spec_references: Castles: Form and Function c.1000-1750 — The location of Kenilworth Castle; The appearance and layout of Kenilworth Castle at different times in its history
key_events_dates: c.1125 — Castle founded by Geoffrey de Clinton
1390s — John of Gaunt's great hall built
lessons.impartiality_notes: Kenilworth Castle is curated by English Heritage. Note site presentation reflects English Heritage editorial choices.

lessons.title: Kenilworth's functions: defence, residence, administration
lessons.description: Royal castle, baronial fortress, comfortable Tudor residence — how Kenilworth's use changed across 750 years.
spec_references: Castles: Form and Function — Day to day function(s) of Kenilworth Castle at different times in its history; Life in Kenilworth Castle at different times in its history
key_events_dates: 1244 — Henry III takes castle into royal hands
1266 — Siege of Kenilworth (longest medieval English siege, ~6 months)
key_figures: Simon de Montfort the Younger (Siege of Kenilworth 1266)
lessons.impartiality_notes: Site-specific factual lesson. Drill the 1266 siege and the 1575 royal visit as iconic moments.

lessons.title: Source skills for Kenilworth and the Reformation
lessons.description: Wills, inventories, churchwardens' accounts and surviving fabric — using mixed evidence on the site paper.
spec_references: Castles: Form and Function — The evidence used by historians; Key events associated with Kenilworth Castle at different times in its history
lessons.impartiality_notes: Drill the 10-mark source comparison structure. Source A vs Source B woven against an investigation question, with site-specific contextual knowledge.

article_units.name: Personal Rule to Restoration 1629-1660 with Kenilworth Castle
article_units.subtitle: Charles I, Civil War, regicide, Cromwell and the restoration of Charles II — plus Kenilworth Castle as historic environment.
article_units.spec_section_focus: British depth study + historic environment, Component 3. 55 marks total. Paired with War and British Society thematic. Kenilworth Castle is the fixed site from 2019 onwards.

lessons.title: Charles I's Personal Rule 1629-1640
lessons.description: Eleven years without Parliament — ship money, Laudian reforms and the rising opposition.
spec_references: Relationship between Parliament and Charles I 1629-1642 — Reasons why Charles I called Parliament in 1640; the Long Parliament's criticisms of Charles I's Personal Rule, including financial and religious measures and suppression of criticism (1629-1640); attacks on Laud and Strafford
lessons.impartiality_notes: Use 'Personal Rule' as the spec's preferred term. The older 'Eleven Years' Tyranny' label is Whig historiography — note it as terminology but don't adopt as default.

lessons.title: Slide to civil war 1640-1642
lessons.description: Grand Remonstrance, the Five Members and Charles raising his standard at Nottingham.
spec_references: Relationship between Parliament and Charles I — events leading to civil war, including rebellion in Ireland in 1641, Grand Remonstrance 1641, attempt on the Five Members 1642, Militia Ordinance 1642, Nineteen Propositions 1642; divisions within Parliament 1640-1642
key_events_dates: 4 Jan 1642 — Charles attempts to arrest Five Members
22 Aug 1642 — Charles raises royal standard at Nottingham
lessons.impartiality_notes: Drill: Five Members = Pym, Hampden, Holles, Haselrig, Strode. Examiner reports reward correct enumeration of named individuals.

lessons.title: First Civil War 1642-1646
lessons.description: Edgehill, Marston Moor, Naseby and the New Model Army — how Parliament beat the King.
spec_references: The political and religious impact of war 1642-1649 — Parliament's attempts to reach agreement with Charles I 1646-1647 (Propositions of Newcastle)
key_events_dates: 1643 — Solemn League and Covenant with Scots
lessons.impartiality_notes: First Civil War deaths estimated at c.85,000 military, c.100,000 civilian (disease, dislocation). State both numbers — civilian cost is often overlooked.

lessons.title: Levellers, Diggers and radical religion
lessons.description: Putney Debates, Diggers on St George's Hill — the army's radical politics after victory.
spec_references: The political and religious impact of war 1642-1649 — reaction of Parliament to the emergence of new religious and political groups, including Levellers, Quakers and Diggers
key_events_dates: Apr 1649 — Diggers begin at St George's Hill
lessons.impartiality_notes: Rainsborough's 'poorest he that is in England hath a life to live as the greatest he' is a documented Putney Debates quote (recorded by Clarke). Drill it accurately. Do not embellish.

lessons.title: Second Civil War, Pride's Purge and regicide
lessons.description: How Charles I went from defeated king to executed traitor in twelve months 1648-1649.
spec_references: The political and religious impact of war 1642-1649 — relationship between Parliament and the Army, including the emergence of the Presbyterian and Independent parties and the debate about settlement with the King; the execution of Charles I 1649; Rump Parliament and the declaration of Republic 1649
key_events_dates: 1648 — Second Civil War (English risings + Scottish invasion)
lessons.impartiality_notes: Regicide divides historiography (e.g. Sean Kelsey, Mark Kishlansky). State legal arguments on both sides — Charles refused to plead, court constituted by Rump only.

lessons.title: Rump Parliament and the rise of Cromwell 1649-1653
lessons.description: Ireland, Scotland, the Dutch War — and the army turning on its own Parliament.
spec_references: The nature and extent of political and religious change 1649-c.1660 — Relationship between Rump Parliament and Cromwell 1649-1653
lessons.impartiality_notes: Cromwell in Ireland: documented Drogheda toll c.3,500. Sensitive in Irish memory. State facts; note that Cromwell himself justified his actions on the laws of war (siege defying surrender) — historians divided on whether justified.

lessons.title: Protectorate 1653-1658
lessons.description: Barebone's Parliament, Instrument of Government, Major-Generals and the Humble Petition.
spec_references: The nature and extent of political and religious change — relationship between Parliament and Cromwell 1653-1658, including the Instrument of Government and rule of the Major Generals; Humble Petition and Advice, and Cromwell's response
key_events_dates: Dec 1653 — Instrument of Government; Cromwell becomes Lord Protector
lessons.impartiality_notes: Present Cromwell's refusal of the crown as documented decision with contested motives. Not a settled question.

lessons.title: Restoration 1658-1660
lessons.description: Richard's resignation, Monck's march south and the return of Charles II — how the republic ended.
spec_references: The nature and extent of political and religious change — attempts to reach a settlement September 1658 – April 1660; restoration of the monarchy, including the terms of Restoration c.1660
key_events_dates: 1659 — Rump restored, then dissolved, then restored
Feb 1660 — Monck marches from Scotland to London
May 1660 — Convention Parliament; Charles II returns
lessons.impartiality_notes: Declaration of Breda is a documentary anchor — drill its four promises (pardon, religious toleration, army pay, land settlement). Most were partially walked back.

lessons.title: Kenilworth Castle in the Civil War
lessons.description: Kenilworth as Parliamentary garrison and the slighting of 1649-50 — the castle's Civil War story.
spec_references: Castles: Form and Function c.1000-1750 — Connections to events including: baronial and other rebellions, border warfare, civil war sieges; The lives of the castle owners; The people who made the castle function
key_events_dates: 1642 — Castle held for Parliament under Sir Edward Peyto
1661 — Estate granted to Sir Edward Hyde
key_figures: Sir Edward Hyde, Earl of Clarendon
lessons.impartiality_notes: Site-specific factual lesson. The slighting is the most exam-relevant moment because it directly connects Kenilworth to the British depth study window.

lessons.title: Source skills for Kenilworth and Personal Rule
lessons.description: Parliamentary diaries, royal proclamations, Civil War pamphlets and English Heritage interpretation.
spec_references: Castles: Form and Function — The evidence used by historians; Key events associated with Kenilworth Castle at different times in its history
lessons.impartiality_notes: Drill the 10-mark source comparison structure. Source A vs Source B woven against an investigation question, with site-specific contextual knowledge. Avoid taking pamphlet propaganda at face value.
